Tonight the beacon has failed, and a passenger ship is heading for a harbour nobody uses.

A new apprentice, Isaac, arrives at the failing lighthouse on Bracken Isle. Keeper Ted opens the door to “the new guy” and, after a beat, sends him down to the basement to shovel coal into the boiler. Overwhelmed by the storm, two sailors, Arthur and Daniel, moor their rowboat at the island’s dock and look for shelter; Ted sees them from the window and tells the apprentice to open the island gate.

2. The storm sets the clock: pressure comes from the world (the approaching ship’s lights, worsening weather, falling visibility, and rocks in the dark), never from a timer, meter, or enemy. Elapsed time drives what the player perceives (sound, lightning, wind, the ship’s lights); phase and route position drive what the player collides with (hazard density). Test: can the player feel time running
Scope rule: small world, read closely. One lighthouse, one stretch of sea, one abandoned harbour (the Saltgate), and no new major locations.

The lighthouse uses warm lamplight against blue-grey storm light. The beam remains a navigational and dramatic anchor. The abandoned Saltgate quays, log fragments, shrines, symbols, and subtly strange architecture suggest a history without settling its cause. Audio favours wind, rain, machinery, buoy bells, and a distant foghorn over musical stingers.

Folk-horror discoveries: the core discoveries are placed in the lighthouse and on the island, before boarding, where there is no ship deadline, and are tied to why the beacon failed. The Saltgate keeps a lighter set. This keeps the signature content outside the timed act. Nothing here is canon or scheduled. Build an item only after the creator approves it, and only if it still fits the four design pillars and the scope rule in the Executive Summary.
More Saltgate detail

Until the prototype is considered complete, the Saltgate stays minimal and no significant detail is added to it. After that, it could carry more folk-horror atmosphere, canon clues and in-world documentation: additional log fragments, shrines, symbols, notes and subtly strange architecture that suggest the history of the island and the earlier keepers without settling its cause.

• First-person 3D with a stylised stormy sea that moves for atmosphere, and a boat steered past rocks, buoys, and debris. Waves that push the boat are a stretch goal, so a built-in ocean is useful but not essential.

1. Godot 4 is the best overall fit (as Technical Strategy proposes): fast iteration, no fees, and text scenes that AI agents can work on directly. With waves now a stretch goal, its main weakness (no built-in ocean) is off the critical path; build waves yourself only if the schedule allows.
The unit is one agent task: a bounded job such as “implement the gate interaction” or “fix the boat clipping through rocks”, including reading files, editing, running the project, and fixing errors.

Use explicit phase states, for example ARRIVAL_AND_COAL → SHELTER_AND_GATE → BEACON_DIAGNOSIS → BOARDING → OUTBOUND → SALTGATE → RETURN → FINAL_REPAIR → RESOLUTION (WIN or FAIL). Start with a constrained, tunable approximation: a forward-moving boat with one fixed speed and one player steering axis. The player steers but has no throttle. The core crossing challenge is steering past placed hazards (rocks, reefs, buoys, and floating debris) along a route that narrows and darkens as the storm worsens. The sea surface animates for atmosphere only and does not push the boat. Ex

Because the boat cannot stop, docking is automatic: arriving within a dock trigger zone at the Saltgate quays or the lighthouse jetty ends steering control and moors the boat, followed by a disembark interaction. If the boat leaves the playable corridor or the player misses the dock approach, the recovery event returns the boat to the last safe point on the route with a time cost. Define each dock

Prototype failure policy: a collision with a rock or debris (or a broadside wave hit, if waves are built) adds water, slows the boat or causes a brief capsize-and-recovery at a nearby safe point; these events consume deadline time once the clock is running (on the outbound crossing they cost no deadline time). On return, cargo mishandling delays progress and creates a clear recovery interaction. P

The shelter and gate sequence is scripted and is part of the Gate 1 slice. After the boiler is fed, Ted prompts the player to look out of the window; Arthur and Daniel’s rowboat is moored at the dock, the sailors overwhelmed by the storm and looking for shelter. There is no crash. Proposed: trigger the moment when the window is in view, with a fallback after a short delay so it cannot be missed. T

The ship first appears at the boarding threshold. It holds at its starting lights until the clock starts. Rules: start on the return-departure event, when the burner is aboard and the boat starts moving

The largest production risk remains boat feel; keeping waves as a stretch goal removes the hardest part of that risk from the critical path. The second is scope creep across repairs, cinematics, and environmental detail, and week 5 loading. Gate 0 and the ten-minute slice should decide whether the full game is feasible before those costs grow.
